title: Quantum Complexity Classes and Oracle Separations

items.title: PromiseBPP
items.statement:
Let $\Pi=(Y,N)$ be a promise problem, so $Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ are disjoint ([[def-promise-problem]]). We say $\Pi$ belongs to $\mathrm{PromiseBPP}$ if there are one fixed probabilistic Turing machine $M$ and one positive integer polynomial $p$ such that every random branch halts within $p(|x|)$ transitions and

$$ \Pr[M(x)\text{ accepts}]\ge \frac23\quad(x\in Y),\qquad \Pr[M(x)\text{ accepts}]\le \frac13\quad(x\in N). $$

The probability is over the uniform finite tape $\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}$ of independent fair bits; after the machine halts, unused suffix bits are ignored, as in [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The pair has no correctness requirement outside $Y\cup N$. For total promise pairs this is the ordinary BPP acceptance convention of [[def-rp-corp-zpp-bpp-and-pp-classes]].

references.title: John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section IV.1
Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2

items.title: Indexed uniform circuits convert to polynomial-time full lists
items.statement: Let $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a polynomial-size Boolean circuit family generated in the indexed-gate, logspace sense of [[def-logspace-uniform-circuit-family]]. Assume a fixed polynomial $q$ bounds the number of non-input nodes of $C_n$ by $q(n)$. There is one deterministic polynomial-time machine which, on unary input $1^n$, writes a complete self-delimiting topological gate list for $C_n$, including its input count, all node records and its designated output. The resulting list describes the same circuit and therefore computes the same Boolean function.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section IV.1

items.axiom_use: None; the proof counts configurations of one deterministic transducer and uses finite output lists.

items.title: Computational-basis instruments and conditional states on two registers
items.statement:
Let $A,B$ be nonzero finite-dimensional registers with ordered orthonormal bases $(e_a)_{a\in\Lambda}$ and $(g_b)_{b\in\Gamma}$. Define $P_a e_{a'}=\delta_{a,a'}e_a$ and $Q_b g_{b'}=\delta_{b,b'}g_b$; tensor products of these maps use [[def-qc-tensor-map]]. The maps

$$ \mathcal I_a(R)=(P_a\otimes I_B)R(P_a\otimes I_B),\qquad \mathcal J_b(R)=(I_A\otimes Q_b)R(I_A\otimes Q_b) $$

form finite instruments on $A\otimes B$. If $\psi=\sum_{a,b}c_{a,b}e_a\otimes g_b$ is a unit vector, then their outcome probabilities are

$$ p_A(a)=\sum_b|c_{a,b}|^2,\qquad p_B(b)=\sum_a|c_{a,b}|^2. $$

For a positive-probability outcome, the conditional state is the rank-one density operator on the normalized projected vector. This applies to measuring either register of the Simon state after its coherent XOR query.

references.title: John Watrous, The Theory of Quantum Information, Section 2.3.2
Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.2

items.axiom_use: None; all outcome sets, registers, and sums are finite.

items.title: EQP on promise problems in the QC14 model
items.statement:
A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{EQP}$ in the QC14 model if there is a full-list uniform family $(C_n)_{n\ge0}$ and a polynomial-time total acceptance predicate $A_n$ as in [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], using the exact gate and cost conventions of [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]] and [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]], such that

$$ p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=1\quad(x\in Y),\qquad p_{C_{|x|}}(x)=0\quad(x\in N). $$

No condition is imposed on $x\notin Y\cup N$ ([[def-promise-problem]]). The finite output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]].

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section IV.1

items.title: ZQP on promise problems with bounded failure
items.statement:
In this page, $\mathrm{ZQP}$ denotes the following bounded-failure zero-error promise class. A promise problem $\Pi=(Y,N)$ belongs to $\mathrm{ZQP}$ if there are a full-list uniform QC14 family $(C_n)$, a polynomial-time total label decoder $D_n(x,z)\in\{\mathrm{YES},\mathrm{NO},?\}$, and the finite output law of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]], [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], and [[def-qc-quantum-acceptance-probability]], such that for every $x\in Y$ the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is zero, while for every $x\in N$ the probability of $\mathrm{NO}$ is at least $2/3$ and the probability of $\mathrm{YES}$ is zero. All output strings receive one of the three labels, so the remaining probability is the allowed failure label $?$; the output law is normalized by [[thm-qc-output-acceptance-law-normalizes]]. No promise condition is imposed off $Y\cup N$.

This explicit fixed-circuit, bounded-failure convention is sufficient for the containments proved on this page. No equivalence with an expected-time quantum zero-error model or with $\mathrm{BQP}\cap\mathrm{coBQP}$ is asserted.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section IV.1

items.title: Boolean circuits compile exactly into the QC14 gate alphabet
items.statement:
Let a finite Boolean DAG in the basis of [[def-boolean-circuit-size-depth-fanin-and-basis]] have $n$ ordered input bits, $m$ ordered output ports, $S$ non-input nodes and $E$ input-port uses counted with multiplicity. There is a deterministic compiler which, from its explicit topological list, emits a valid QC14 circuit over exactly $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$ with the first $n$ wires as data, $m$ zero-initialized target wires, at most $S+E$ clean value wires and one additional clean scratch wire. For every $x\in\{0,1\}^n$ and $y\in\{0,1\}^m$, its unitary satisfies

$$ |x,y,0^{S+E+1}\rangle\longmapsto |x,y\oplus f(x),0^{S+E+1}\rangle, $$

where $f(x)$ is the ordered Boolean output. It uses at most $27(6S+4E+m)$ QC14 gate occurrences, and the full self-delimiting circuit list is produced in time polynomial in the Boolean-DAG description length. The same action holds on superpositions by linearity.

references.title: John Preskill, Quantum Computation, Chapter 5: Classical and Quantum Circuits, Sections 5.2.2–5.2.3
Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Sections 2.1.2–2.3

items.axiom_use: None; the compilation is a finite gate replacement and uses no choice.

items.title: BQP to PP and PSPACE proof obligations in the exact QC14 basis
items.statement:
## Remarks

The established containments $\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PP}$ and $\mathrm{BQP}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}$ remain proof obligations for the exact QC14 gate alphabet $H,T,T^\dagger,\mathrm{CNOT}$, whose entries lie in $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)=\mathbb Q(i,\sqrt2)$ ([[def-qc-bqp-promise-class]], [[def-qc-clifford-t-gate-library]]). The PP route must encode amplitudes and acceptance weights over this number field, prove the required GapP closure, and compare against the strict $1/2$ threshold. The BQP thresholds $2/3$ and $1/3$ differ by $1/3$; each is at distance $1/6$ from $1/2$ (equivalently, $2p-1$ has margin at least $1/3$). A rational path count cannot simply replace the exact $\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)$ computation, since the probabilities can contain $\sqrt2$. The PSPACE route needs exact-field or certified-precision recursive evaluation with explicit bit-length and space bounds for each arithmetic and threshold step. The source containment arguments are context, not local proof suppliers; no containment item is claimed here.

references.title: John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section III
Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Sections 13.2–13.3

items.title: PromiseP is contained in EQP, EQP in ZQP, and ZQP in BQP
items.statement:
In the QC14 promise-problem model,

$$ \mathrm{PromiseP}\subseteq\mathrm{EQP}\subseteq\mathrm{ZQP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}. $$

Here $\mathrm{ZQP}$ has the bounded-failure, no-wrong-definite-answer convention of [[def-qa-32-zqp-promise-class]], and $\mathrm{BQP}$ uses the exact $2/3,1/3$ thresholds of [[def-qc-bqp-promise-class]].

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Sections IV.1–IV.3

items.axiom_use: None; the compiler and output predicates are finite and deterministic.

items.title: PromiseP is contained in PromiseBPP and PromiseBPP in BQP
items.statement:
For promise problems in the QC14 model,

$$ \mathrm{PromiseP}\subseteq\mathrm{PromiseBPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}, \qquad \mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}. $$

references.title: John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Sections IV.1 and IV.3
Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 13, Section 13.2

items.axiom_use: None; random tapes, circuit families, and compiler outputs are finite and explicitly encoded.

items.title: Simon injectivity decision promise with XOR-oracle access
items.statement:
Fix $n\ge1$ and put $V_n=\{0,1\}^n$, with coordinatewise addition $\oplus$ over $\mathbb F_2$ and cardinality $N=2^n$. For $s,y\in V_n$, define the dot product $s\cdot y=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}s_jy_j\pmod 2$. A table code consists of a unary header $1^n0$ followed by the $n$-bit words $f(x)$ in lexicographic order of $x\in V_n$; this identifies function instances with binary strings as in [[def-promise-problem]], [[def-finite-field-and-its-order]], and [[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]].

The YES promise set $Y_n$ consists of table codes of injective maps $f:V_n\to V_n$. The NO promise set $N_n$ consists of codes for which there is a nonzero $s\in V_n$ such that, for every $x,y\in V_n$,

$$ f(x)=f(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=x\ \text{or}\ y=x\oplus s. $$

The sets are disjoint: every NO function has a collision between the distinct inputs $x$ and $x\oplus s$. Its mask is unique, since two different nonzero masks would give a third distinct input in the same fiber. Classical query access returns $f(x)$ at a chosen address. Quantum query access is the coherent XOR oracle $U_f|x,z\rangle=|x,z\oplus f(x)\rangle$ of [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], which is unitary and involutive by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]]. Each call is one query; query charges remain separate from ordinary gate costs by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. In the query model the table is not supplied as gate data; the table code fixes the promised function only.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Sections 3.1–3.3
Andrew M. Childs, Lecture Notes on Quantum Algorithms, Chapter 1, Section 1.6
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Sections I and V

items.title: Simon promise decision by sampled rank
items.statement:
Input: an integer $n\ge1$ and oracle access to a promised function $f:V_n\to V_n$ from [[def-qa-32-simon-decision-oracle-promise]]. Set $m=n+2$. For each of $m$ independent runs, initialize two ordered $n$-qubit registers $X,Y$ to $|0^n\rangle|0^n\rangle$, apply $H^{\otimes n}$ to $X$, and query the coherent XOR oracle $U_f$ once on $X,Y$. Apply the computational-basis instrument on $Y$ from [[lem-qa-32-simon-function-register-instrument]], record and discard its classical outcome, apply $H^{\otimes n}$ again to $X$, and measure $X$ in the computational basis using the same instrument. Record the resulting $y_j\in V_n$.

Form the $m\times n$ binary matrix with rows $y_1,\ldots,y_m$. Set the next pivot row to $r=1$ and scan columns $j=1,\ldots,n$ from left to right. In column $j$, search rows $r,\ldots,m$ for the first row with a $1$ in that column. If there is no such row, leave the column without a pivot and continue to the next column. Otherwise swap that row with row $r$, XOR row $r$ into every other row with a $1$ in column $j$, and increase $r$ by one. Accept (declare injective) exactly when the number of pivots is $n$.

This procedure uses exactly $n+2$ oracle queries, $2n(n+2)$ ordinary Hadamard gates, two finite measurement readouts per run, and $O(n^3)$ classical bit operations for elimination. A query is charged separately from an implementation of $f$ by [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]]. It makes no gate-time separation claim.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.2
Andrew M. Childs, Lecture Notes on Quantum Algorithms, Chapter 1, Section 1.6

items.title: Classical randomized Simon decision requires square-root-many queries
items.statement: Let $N=2^n$ with $n\ge4$. A classical randomized adaptive algorithm that, given only classical query access $x\mapsto f(x)$ to the Simon decision promise of [[def-qa-32-simon-decision-oracle-promise]], must decide injective versus nonzero-mask two-to-one with worst-case error at most $1/3$ requires $\Omega(\sqrt N)=\Omega(2^{n/2})$ queries. Ordinary classical computation between queries is unrestricted.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.3.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Sections I and V

items.axiom_use: None; the oracle families and randomized decision trees are finite.

items.title: Simon rank test correctness and linear query cost
items.statement:
For every $n\ge1$, the sample in [[alg-qa-32-simon-query-rank-test]] is uniform on $V_n$ when $f$ is YES, and uniform on $s^\perp=\{y:s\cdot y=0\}$ when $f$ is NO with mask $s\ne0$. The rank test rejects every NO instance. On YES its error probability is at most

$$ (2^n-1)2^{-(n+2)}<\frac14. $$

It uses exactly $n+2$ queries and $O(n^3)$ classical bit operations.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.2
John Watrous, Quantum Computational Complexity, Section IV.1

items.axiom_use: None; the proof uses only finite sums, finite probability spaces, and explicit bit-vector operations.

title: Quantum Complexity Classes and Oracle Separations — Examples

items.title: Simon query lower bounds do not imply explicit-input gate lower bounds
items.statement: For the Simon decision promise, the classical-versus-quantum oracle-query separation implies that the same promise problem, with an explicit full truth-table input of length $L$, has no deterministic algorithm running in time polynomial in $L$.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.3.2
Andrew M. Childs, Lecture Notes on Quantum Algorithms, Chapter 1, Section 1.6

items.title: Simon decision for n equals two
items.statement: Take $n=2$, so $V_2=\mathbb F_2^2$, and consider a NO function with mask $s=01$. Then $s^\perp=\{00,10\}$, so every Simon sample lies in this one-dimensional subspace and the rank test rejects. On a YES permutation, the algorithm takes $m=n+2=4$ independent uniform samples. Its exact probability of failing to span is $23/128$, and the general union bound is $3/16$.

references.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, Section 3.2
